newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet accident hearing gets underway.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet accident hearing gets underway.

text.p: The National Transportation Safety Board was meeting Tuesday to consider its final report on the crash last year of ValuJet flight 592 that killed 110 people.

The DC-9 plunged into the Florida Everglades on May 11, 1996. Preliminary reports show the crash was caused by a fire in the cargo hold fueled by oxygen-generating canisters that were improperly handled and labeled.
NTSB Chairman James Hall has already described the accident as one that need not have happened if the board's warnings about the dangers of cargo fires had been heeded.

In a statement prepared for the NTSB meeting, investigator-in-charge, Gregory Feith, said that of the 25 oxygen generators found at the accident site, many bore internal and external evidence of fire and heat damage.
An agenda for the meeting listed the role of ValuJet and its contractor, SabreTech Corp., in the accident as well as the oversight of the Federal Aviation Administration as matters for consideration.
Last week ValuJet said there was significant evidence that some SabreTech employees deliberately and deceptively mislabeled the oxygen generators.
SabreTech denied the allegations saying there was no evidence that anyone deliberately deceived ValuJet.
ValuJet is to merge shortly with AirWays Corp. and will be renamed AirTran Airlines.
Feith's statement said employees at SabreTech were told to clean up their facility before a customer made an inspection.
As part of that cleanup, 144 oxygen generators were packed into five boxes and put aboard flight 592 marked as company material and listed on the cargo manifest as "oxy cannisters - empty".

The ValuJet crash has already led to changes at the FAA, including closer scrutiny of new, rapidly expanding carriers and banning the carrying of oxygen generators in the cargo holds of passenger aircraft.
The oxygen generators are considered safe when located above passengers as a source of emergency oxygen if depressurization occurs during flight.
The FAA recently ordered airlines to install smoke alarm systems but gave them three years to do it, a period Hall has suggested was too long.
Aviation safety sources believe the fire may have started before the ValuJet plane took off and a smoke alarm could have warned the crew.
"This goes back to a 1988 recommendation the board made (on fitting fire detection and suppression equipment)," Hall said on Sunday.
"Had that recommendation been implemented, it is certainly questionable whether the ValuJet accident would have happened at all," he said.
Hall called on airlines to voluntarily install the new cargo hold equipment ahead of the FAA's three-year timetable.
